name: libaacs
desc: Implements the Advanced Access Content System specification
why: Implements the AACS disc encryption spec, a fascinating window into how Blu-ray content protection works.

brief.what_it_is: libaacs is an open-source library that implements the Advanced Access Content System (AACS) specification, the content protection scheme used on Blu-ray discs. The homepage describes it as a research project for understanding how AACS works. It ships with an executable named aacs_info, which the Homebrew metadata lists but the homepage does not describe. The homepage does not say what inputs it takes or what output it produces beyond the library itself. It is not a decryption tool: the project states it provides no keys or certificates.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a research project to make AACS understandable through readable open-source code. It also calls the project fun to hack on because it is DRM and crypto-related.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says the main dependency is libgcrypt, which handles all cryptographic functions. It does not explain the internal mechanism of the AACS implementation. I could not read the repository README because the code host returned an Anti-bot challenge page.

commands_seen.context: Clones the libaacs source repository from the VideoLAN GitLab, given on the homepage as the Git option for getting the code.

brief.install_notes: The homepage lists a download server for the latest release, libaacs 0.12.0, and the git clone above as an alternative. The main dependency is libgcrypt. The homepage gives no build steps, configuration, or accounts. The repository page itself was blocked, so build instructions from the README are unknown.
brief.standout: Most libraries in this space exist to play or rip media. This one is explicitly a research and education project that publishes no keys or certificates, and it treats the DRM as something to study and hack on.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but the evidence is thin. The homepage names libaacs 0.12.0 as the latest release and links a download server and an active Git repository. I found no release date or last-commit date, so the exact status is unknown.
brief.caveats: Supported platforms are listed as GNU/Linux, Windows, and macOS X. The library includes no keys or certificates, so it cannot decrypt discs on its own. The homepage has a legal disclaimer saying it does not infringe DRM rights or copyright. The code host (code.videolan.org) returned an Anubis proof-of-work challenge that requires JavaScript, so I could not read the repository README. The homepage was reachable.

judge.reason: A readable implementation of Blu-ray’s content-protection system offers an unusual way to explore DRM and cryptography, even without bundled keys or certificates.

entry.title: libaacs
entry.tldr: An open-source library implementing the AACS copy protection scheme used on Blu-ray discs, published as a research project for understanding how DRM and its crypto fit together.
entry.deeper_look:
libaacs implements the Advanced Access Content System (AACS) specification, the content protection scheme used on Blu-ray discs. Its homepage describes it as a research project that provides, in the project's words, "through an open-source library, a way to understand how the AACS works." The idea is that a protection scheme you can read as code is one you can study.

The project is not a decryption tool. The homepage says it offers no keys or certificates that could be used to decode encrypted copyrighted material, and it carries a legal disclaimer saying it does not infringe DRM rights or copyright. On its own, the library cannot unlock a disc. What it gives you is the structure of the system in readable form.

All cryptographic functions go through libgcrypt, the library's main dependency. The homepage does not explain the internals of the AACS implementation, so the code itself is where the learning is. The project also calls itself "a fun project to hack on, because it is DRM and crypto-related", which is an honest pitch: key hierarchies, licensing, and revocation are an unusual puzzle to read through.

Homebrew installs one executable, aacs_info. The homepage does not describe it, so what it takes as input and prints is not confirmed here. Start with its help output.
entry.install:
brew install libaacs
# depends on libgcrypt and libgpg-error, which brew pulls in
# Source alternative: git clone https://code.videolan.org/videolan/libaacs.git (build steps not confirmed)

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage text for the one executable the formula installs, which is the quickest way to learn what it expects.
Fetches the library source from VideoLAN's GitLab so you can read how AACS is put together.

entry.whats_unique: Most libraries in this space exist to play or rip media. This one presents itself as research and education, ships no keys or certificates, and treats the DRM as something to study.
entry.caveats: It cannot decrypt discs by itself since it includes no keys, and what aacs_info does is undocumented on the homepage; maintenance status is unclear, with 0.12.0 named as the latest release but no dates found.
